newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: No-go zone imposed around NZ's Mount Ruapehu crate.
newsitem.headline: No-go zone imposed around NZ's Mount Ruapehu crate.

text.p: New Zealand scientists on Tuesday went on alert for fresh eruptions from Mount Ruapehu, a volcano on the central North Island.
The Department of Conservation (DOC) reimposed restrictions on access around the summit of the 2,800-metre (9,000-foot) high, snow-clad crater following an increase in seismic activity.
The Turoa and Whakapapa ski fields on the mountain lie outside the "warning zone".
DOC scientist Harry Keys said the mountain had been freshly shaken by low-level tremors, starting on Saturday, in the first significant seismic activity since August 1996.
The imposing mountain burst into life in the last two southern winters, spewing ash over large swathes of the North Island, disrupting air traffic and closing the mountain to skiers.

The weekend tremors, lasting 31 hours, had subsided for now but could increase again, Keys said, adding that they raised the possibility of an eruption as they indicated magma, or molten rock, was on the move beneath the mountain.
He noted, however, that there was so little water in the crater lake that there was a low risk of a lahar -- a mudflow.
The crater lake emptied last year during the eruptions.
Institute of Nuclear and Geological Sciences spokesman Brad Scott agreed that the tremors pointed to a possible eruption.
"The fact that the magma has started (moving inside the volcano) increases the probability or possibility of an eruption... It could come back in a hour."
When magma erupts from a volcano it becomes lava.
Both DOC and the Nuclear Sciences Institute said they were keeping a close watch on the mountain.
Scott said the 1996 eruptions were preceded by a strong volcanic tremor, about 36 hours before the eruption started.
The tremor recorded this weekend was lower in amplitude than that recorded before the 1996 eruptions, but occurred over a longer period.
